summary: Weekly POC sync focused on token economics and performance tuning. Review of last week's runs showed large gains from prefix/KV caching for common prompts; batching improved throughput but increased tail latency. Agreed next steps are a 6h canary benchmark with controlled batch sizes and prefix caching enabled, Praxis will send actual prompt set, Redwood to share security docs and a conservative routing fallback for production rollouts.
transcript:
[00:00:00] Sofia (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. Quick roll call — Marcus from SE, Priya, Tom, Leila from Praxis, are we good?
[00:00:08] Priya (Praxis): Yep, good to go. Thanks.
[00:00:12] Marcus (SE): Morning/afternoon all. We pushed the KV prefix caching patch last night and ran the 3 hour job.
[00:00:20] Tom (Praxis): Yup we saw the reports, there were some big numbers in there. I, uh, had a couple questions on the baseline though.
[00:00:30] Sofia: Cool. Let's run through the headline numbers first. Marcus, can you summarize what changed and delta on tokens per dollar?
[00:00:38] Marcus: Sure. Baseline was without prefix caching, batching at 4, model variant is mid-size open-llama-esque checkpoint we agreed on. Baseline tokens/sec/$ we measured about 0.9 — which is kind of in line with earlier runs. After turning on prefix/KV caching for the top-20 prompts we saw tokens/sec/$ increase to ~2.6 — so roughly 2.8x improvement. Note: that's for steady-state traffic with high prompt redundancy.
[00:01:05] Leila (Praxis): Wait 2.6 tokens per second per dollar? Can you restate the unit — we got mixed up with tokens per dollar earlier.
[00:01:12] Marcus: Yeah, sorry. We're using tokens/sec/$ as a comparative metric — think of it as throughput normalized by spend. Previously we'd get about 0.9, now 2.6. If you prefer tokens per dollar total, that's about 38k tokens per dollar in the cached scenario vs ~11k before.
[00:01:30] Priya: That maps to what we saw in the sheet, thanks. Where is the biggest win coming from — is it KV cache hit rate?
[00:01:37] Marcus: Exactly. For the top-20 prompts hit rate is ~72% after the prefix normalization step. That avoids full forward passes for the common prefix, reduces token generation per query and cuts compute.
[00:01:48] Tom: On the infra side we noticed GPU utilization went down but token-per-cost improved — is that because the runtime is doing less work per call?
[00:01:55] Marcus: Right. Lower per-request work (because of cached KV segments) means fewer tokens executed on GPU per request, so utilization drops but effective tokens per dollar goes up. It's an efficiency improvement, not capable-of-more-requests per second in absolute if you have cold unique prompts.
[00:02:08] Sofia: Let's talk batching — earlier you had a set of runs with batch 4,8,16. What were the throughput and latency tradeoffs there?
[00:02:15] Marcus: With batching only (no cache) going from 4->8 gave ~1.9x throughput gain and median latency went from ~95ms to ~130ms. 8->16 gave an extra 1.4x throughput but median latency jumped to ~210ms and p95 moved to ~740ms — tail got worse. When we combined caching + batching, effective throughput for cache-hits increased more because cache hits are fast and pack nicely, but for cache-misses the tail is worse at batch=16.
[00:02:45] Priya: Our product SLO is 200ms median and 800ms p95, so batch=16 might push us over p95 occasionally.
[00:02:53] Leila: Are we able to differentiate routing: use batch=16 for background/high-throughput low-latency tolerant routes, and batch=4 for interactive routes?
[00:03:01] Marcus: Exactly, that's a classic routing policy. Redwood runtime supports per-route batching config and fallback to smaller batch sizes for routes with latency constraints. We can also do per-user or token-threshold policies.
[00:03:12] Tom: Any quantization or model variant changes that affect these numbers? Last week you mentioned a 4-bit quantized variant.
[00:03:18] Marcus: Yes. We ran the same battery on a q4 variant. Raw throughput improved slightly (about +10-15% tokens/sec) but quality/regression checks showed wobble on a handful of prompts; we flagged those in the eval. Cost-wise q4 reduces compute cost per token so tokens/sec/$ improved another ~20% in cached scenario. But if you need strict output fidelity, we might stick to the non-quantized or do selective quantization.
[00:03:40] Priya: Do we have a simple rule-of-thumb to recommend to the product team? Like for conversational assistant keep q8 and batch=4, for background generation use q4 + batch=16?
[00:03:50] Marcus: I'd phrase it: interactive (latency sensitive) -> smaller batches (1-6), prefer higher-fidelity variant; high-throughput async -> larger batches (8-32), quantized variants okay. Also enable prefix caching for any route with >20% repeated prefixes.
[00:04:06] Sofia: Great. Let's call out cost math for the exec team — Marcus you mentioned 38k tokens per dollar with caching and q4 gave an extra 20% — so around 45k tokens per dollar if we combine both?
[00:04:16] Marcus: Roughly yes, caveat: that's for our test cluster (mixed GPUs) and the actual number will shift depending on hardware + sequence lengths.
[00:04:24] Leila: Sequence length — we generally average 420 tokens per request in production, but the pilot used 280; will that change numbers dramatically?
[00:04:31] Marcus: It does. Longer sequences increase KV cache utility (more shared prefixes) but also increase per-request compute. For tokens/sec/$ the delta depends on prefix overlap. If you have longer tails with unique content, the efficiency drops. We'll need your 24h traffic sample to simulate real distribution.
[00:04:46] Tom: There was one anomaly in the last run — a spike in latency around 11:23 UTC, any idea?
[00:04:52] Marcus: Looking at the traces it was an autoscaler event combined with a cold KV fill. Cold fills cost extra and that aligned with a background scaling operation. We recommended a small pre-warm window and sticky routing for active sessions.
[00:05:04] Sofia: That ties into the dedicated vs hosted question — Praxis has asked about a private deployment for compliance. How does that change economics?
[00:05:11] Marcus: Private deployments reduce cross-tenant optimizations — you lose some multi-tenant packing but you gain network predictability. Cost per token may go up ~10-30% depending on commit level and utilization, but you get data isolation and KMS integration. There are also dedicated caching layers you can control which sometimes improves hit rates.
[00:05:28] Priya: If we do dedicated with reserved capacity, do you have guidance on commit sizing? We don't want to overcommit.
[00:05:34] Marcus: We usually recommend a glide path: reserved baseline for 60-70% of expected steady load and autoscale for bursts. For pilots we size to observed steady qps during peak hours and then run a 2-week stress to inform commit. Redwood Console gives token and cost breakdown per route so you can adjust.
[00:05:46] Leila: Can we see a sample routing policy for the interactive assistant vs batch background job?
[00:05:51] Sofia: I'll send a snippet after the call. Marcus, quick — do you have anything to add on caching TTLs and invalidation?
[00:05:58] Marcus: TTLs depend on business semantics — for prompts that change often, keep TTL low (30-60s), static templates can be days. We also support explicit invalidation via API. For the pilot we used a 5-minute TTL and manual invalidation when the model was updated.
[00:06:12] Tom: One operational ask — we need clearer audit logs for which prefixes hit cache and which were misses for compliance. Does Redwood expose that?
[00:06:18] Marcus: Yes, audit logs include event-level cache hit/miss, route, user token (obfuscated) and timing. We can enable an extended retention in the Console (add-on).
[00:06:28] Priya: On next steps you mentioned a canary run. What's the target configuration?
[00:06:33] Marcus: Proposed: 6h run, batch sizes [4,8,16], q8 and q4 variants, prefix cache on for top-20 prompts, TTL=300s. We'll capture tokens/sec/$, median/p95 latency, GPU utilization and cold-hit counts. We'll upload CSV and a short write-up.
[00:06:47] Leila: Sounds good. Also can you include a column for prefix-hit-rate per prompt?
[00:06:51] Marcus: Yep will add that.
[00:06:54] Sofia: Any blockers on data sharing? Praxis needs to sanitize the prompt set, Tom?
[00:06:58] Tom: We'll scrub PII and send redacted. Should be fine.
[00:07:02] Priya: One more question on price — can you give us a ballpark of dedicated monthly costs for a small reserve (2-3 gpus equivalent)?
[00:07:09] Sofia: Ballpark, a small reserved pool starts in the mid-five-figure per month range depending on GPU spec, with commit discounts for 12mo. I'll include a ballpark spreadsheet in the follow-up.
[00:07:18] Leila: Great. Any other concerns?
[00:07:21] Tom: On our side I'll check egress constraints and VPC peering doc, vote to have the security call next week.
[00:07:27] Sofia: Perfect — we'll send the items: benchmark CSV, routing snippet, security pack, and dedicated ballpark.
[00:07:34] Marcus: Quick note on fallback: we can set a policy to failover to smaller batch or different variant if p95 > threshold, or fall back regionally. We'll prototype a conservative policy.
[00:07:45] Priya: Ok let's wrap — do we have DS for the pilot?
[00:07:49] Sofia: Action items captured, thanks everyone. We'll reconvene after the 6h run and target a follow-up on 2026-07-06.
[00:07:55] Leila: Thanks all.
[00:07:57] End of recording.

Notes: Shared artifacts referenced during call - Benchmark sheet: https://redwood.app/sheets/praxis-pilot-bench | Routing snippet (Gist): https://gist.github.com/redwood/praxis-routing | Security pack (short): https://redwood.app/security/praxis-pack
